set.note: First meant simply 'deadly'; Samuel Johnson's dictionary recast it as 'mutually destructive.' Today it usually describes infighting within a group.

why: Earliest English sense (from Latin internecinus) was 'deadly, destructive'; 'deadly to both sides' came from Johnson's 1755 misreading of inter-, so 'originally meant deadly to both sides' is inaccurate
'was pure chicanery' fits the salesman cloze; def overlaps (clever deception)
'dismissed ... as empty platitudes' is a stock phrase that fits the cloze
'the perfume was so heavy and redolent' also fits the cloze sensibly
'could stymie your recovery' also fits the cloze sensibly
'after an hour of entreating from his friends' also fits the cloze; meanings overlap (urging someone to do something)
'parents cajoled the runners to keep going' is a plausible fill; 'implore' means to beg, not a true synonym of exhort
'answered with nothing but vague platitudes' fits the cloze sensibly
'the locker room filled with angry acrimony' is a plausible fill; meanings overlap
'correcting a friend mid-toast was pure chutzpah' is a plausible fill
'our ebullient seatmate chatted nonstop' also fits the cloze sensibly
'meetings grew so bellicose that members shouted' is a plausible fill; meanings overlap (quarrelsome/combative)
acerbic (harsh, biting) overlaps with argumentative/bad-tempered and could be read as fitting the yelling-neighbor cloze
'the team's lackadaisical season ended with zero wins' is a plausible fill
'generalist' is not a synonym: a generalist has broad but not necessarily deep knowledge, which is the distinction the def draws
